title: NASA blasted an asteroid with a spacecraft to change its course 4 years ago. We just got our first glimpse at the aftermath.
excerpt: The 2021 Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission was meant to see whether a human-made object could change an asteroid's path should one in the future be on a collision course with Earth.
content:
Four years ago, NASA ran a test that could one day save humanity. The space agency slammed a spacecraft into the side of a small asteroid to see how effectively it could change its course, which could come in handy in the future should a similar object be on a direct collision course with Earth. 

The test worked. NASA found that the collision had changed the amount of time the asteroid, a football-stadium hunk of space rock called Dimorphos, took to orbit a nearby larger asteroid by 32 minutes. Before the test, the agency said an alteration of 73 seconds or more would be considered a success.

Though NASA was able to judge how much it moved Dimorphos off its previous course, it took an entirely separate mission to provide the first look at what the impact did to the asteroid's surface.

On Wednesday, the European Space Agency (ESA) released the first images of Dimorphos captured by its Hera spacecraft, which was launched in late 2024 to observe Dimorphos and its larger parent asteroid, Didymos, in the wake of NASA's collision test. ESA scientists overseeing the Hera mission described their takeaways from the images at a press conference in Berlin.

"Basically, there were two categories [of potential outcomes]," Patrick Michel, Hera principal investigator, said. "Either we do a small crater or we entirely reshape the asteroid. And in fact, what we find is we have both. We have a crater … that is so large that it extends over the width of the entire asteroid."

The impact has also left Dimorphos "tumbling wildly in its orbit," according to Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

Impact craters on large asteroids are common, but there's a limit to how much scientists can learn from observing them when they don't know the exact size, speed and trajectory of the object that created them. A human-made crater can provide far more insight.

"This offers a unique opportunity to study the physics of impacts at the scale of an asteroid," Michaël Marsset, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory in Germany, told the Guardian. 

How NASA redirected an asteroid

NASA launched its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission in November 2021 on a crash course with Dimorphos. After 10 months of transit through space, the 1,260-pound DART spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos while traveling at roughly 14,000 miles per hour on Sept. 26, 2022.

A few weeks later, NASA announced that the mission had been an unquestioned success, changing the path of Dimorphos's orbit by more than 25 times the minimum change required for success. 

"All of us have a responsibility to protect our home planet. After all, it's the only one we have," then-NASA Administrator Bill Nelson said at the time. "This mission shows that NASA is trying to be ready for whatever the universe throws at us. NASA has proven we are serious as a defender of the planet. This is a watershed moment for planetary defense and all of humanity, demonstrating commitment from NASA's exceptional team and partners from around the world."

In addition to shifting the asteroid's trajectory, the impact released tons of "ejecta" into space. Studying these hunks of displaced rock, many of which remain in orbit around Dimorphos, is another part of Hera's core mission.
